title: US Ambassador Johnson Acts Like a Meddling Policeman, AMLO Says
author: Alexia Villaseñor and Alonso Urrutia
content:
_This article by[Alexia Villaseñor and Alonso
Urrutia](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Alexia%20Villase%C3%B1or%20y%20Alonso%20Urrutia)
originally appeared in the [October 5, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/05/politica/las-cosas-no-
andan-bien-con-gobierno-de-eu-senala-lopez-obrador-en-pueblo), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

No longer bound by the responsibility of the presidential office, in his book
_Pueblo_ , former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador questions the terms of
the bilateral relationship that the United States has sought to impose on
Mexico over these two years. Particularly harsh in his assessment of the
performance of the new ambassador, Ronald Johnson, in this first stage of the
government of Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, he states that this official:

> is neither a diplomat nor a politician; rather, he acts like an excited and
> meddling policeman. He should be more even-tempered and less overbearing,
> seek to resemble Josephus Daniels more and the sinister Henry Lane Wilson
> less. In foreign policy one should not pontificate on someone else's
> territory.
>
> Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Pueblo

The former president accuses Johnson that when the **illegal participation of
the CIA in Chihuahua** was discovered, which contravenes any relationship of
bilateral respect, he reacted in a “defiant tone, neither diplomatic nor much
less political.” The diplomat even threatened that the United States
government would proceed to file complaints in the courts of his country
against alleged Mexican money launderers or corrupt politicians linked to drug
trafficking.

## Withdrawal of His Son's Visa, “Dogmatic and Villainous”

In the chapter “Foreign Policy and Defense of Sovereignty,” López Obrador also
condemns the conduct of the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, considering that
the decision to withdraw the visa –the only mention of the subject– “from my
son Andrés Manuel without any motive or reason” was made in a “dogmatic and
villainous” tenor.

López Obrador writes that neither Ambassador Johnson nor his superiors would
like Mexico to act in the same terms in which they have, that is, that any
Mexican citizen “file complaints in our country with great fanfare against
high-level United States officials who receive money for their electoral
campaigns from arms manufacturers that take the lives of our fellow citizens.”

The former president launches in _Pueblo_ a set of questions about U.S.
conduct. He asks whether that country's rulers would agree to trials being
initiated in Mexico against personnel of their agencies linked to drug
traffickers or for carrying out espionage in our country.

He also asks whether it would agree to allow smuggled weapons to enter to
murder Mexicans and Americans, as happened in Operation _Fast and Furious_.
And whether the United States would endorse Mexicans bringing in people
kidnapped on its territory accused of drug distribution. Or whether they would
like U.S. businessmen to be detained here who have paid bribes to Mexican
officials or are owners or executives of companies that evade taxes.

Unlike the diplomatic terms with which he referred to the Donald Trump
government during his administration, in _Pueblo_ , López Obrador reproaches
that the interference of the United States embassy and the agencies (CIA, DEA
and FBI) has become **much more evident and illegal** under the excuse of
combating drug trafficking, when in reality it is a political matter. In the
book he reproduces the letter he wrote at his ranch La Chingada, in which he
warned of “Trump's surprising change”; he mentioned that “his false friends
and internal advisers” have been dragging him “into vile and sinister
adventures.”

The former president attributes these actions to the annoyance that Mexico has
a popular and progressive government, because they prefer an authoritarian,
disorderly and corrupt one that is vulnerable and docile before their aim of
dominating the country, he says, or perhaps it is influenced by the fact that
certain politicians are bound together by conservative ideology and are bent
on creating a right-wing international association.

## “Dirty Conduct”

For López Obrador, this “dirty conduct” of the U.S. government originates in a
political or electioneering matter, to impress or continue manipulating its
citizens with the accusation that Mexico is the cause of drug addiction in the
neighboring country. And that they, those of the ruling party, are putting an
end to the migration of bad people and drug traffickers who poison their young
people.

He mentioned the “**fabrication of case files with phony evidence** ” in their
effort to accuse the governor on leave of Sinaloa, Rubén Rocha Moya, Senator
Enrique Inzunza and eight other officials of links to drug trafficking.

In that context, he vindicates the response of Sheinbaum, who warned that if
the corresponding evidence were presented, there would be no impunity, but if
it were a complaint of a propagandistic nature, “the blackmail, the reprisal
and the interference of the United States government” would be denounced.

After mentioning the U.S. actions against the governor of Sinaloa, in April,
López Obrador discredits the conduct of the United States government: they
have applied “the almost usual _modus operandi_ , that is, the use of
protected witnesses, their publicity handling, leaks and slander, as well as
the use of tailor-made scripts that their lawyers hand to the accused, that
is, the fabrication of case files with phony evidence, reward or punishment or
many other old tricks.”

Unlike his past allusions to “licenciado Peña Nieto” when he was president,
López Obrador states that he “did nothing to change neoliberal policy or stop
corruption, on the contrary, he deepened it. With him, the decline accelerated
because instead of rectifying, he deepened the neoliberal model. In just two
years, Peña Nieto managed to crudely impose servile compliance with the agenda
dictated from abroad in collusion with the power groups in Mexico –the so-
called labor, education, fiscal and energy reforms–.”

And although he grants that corruption in his government was less than under
Carlos Salinas, in Peña Nieto's six-year term it was “more ostentatious and
uncontrolled.” López Obrador considers that the “failure of Peña's government”
favored his broad chances of winning in 2018, although the journey was not
easy because the oligarchs maintained their determination not to let him
through.

In _Pueblo_ , with **more than 700 pages distributed in 10 chapters** , he
makes a tight summary of the conditions in which his movement was
consolidated, based on his opposition to the neoliberal policies that
prevailed from Miguel de la Madrid to Peña Nieto. To each of them he dedicated
the chapter “PRIAN Neo-Porfirism,” with specific sections for each of them.

He places particular emphasis on the “spurious government of Felipe Calderón,”
whose administration meant more of the same, with the aggravating factor that
the war on drug trafficking was unleashed, which increased violence and
homicides during what he calls the funeral six-year term.

About Salinas, the Tabasco native recounts that in a conversation with a
multimillionaire he asked him who was the richest former president: “he didn't
even blink and answered me immediately: Salinas.”
